questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman presented with fever, bloody diarrhea, and right leg pain. Her symptoms had started 5 days earlier, and her diarrhea was starting to improve (frequency reduced to 2–3 stools/day). She was known to have peripheral vascular disease and hypertension. She kept reptiles as pets. Stool cultures yielded a nontyphoidal Salmonella species.
questions.lead_in: What is a risk factor for invasive disease?
questions.explanation: Atherosclerotic disease The patient is likely to have acquired Salmonella spp . infection from her reptiles, which can act as a reservoir for infection. Patients younger than 12 months have a high risk of neurologic infection and mortality and often may not appear unwell. It is recommended that children <5 years and immunocompromised patients should avoid contact with reptiles. Invasive disease occurs in those who are immunosuppressed and in those aged over 50 years where due to atherosclerotic disease they have a high risk (10%) of endovascular infection if bacteremia develops. Persistent fever, hospital admission, and cardiac or other valvular disease are also risk factors. This patient may also have disseminated Salmonella infection and osteomyelitis of her leg should be excluded.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q16

questions.question: Mycotic aneurysm and its microbial causes.

parts.text: What are the three most common infectious causes of a mycotic aneurysm?

parts_raw.text: What are the 3 most common infectious causes of a mycotic aneurysm?

questions.model_answer: (1) Staphylococcus aureus. (2) Salmonella species (especially non-typhoidal Salmonella in atherosclerotic aorta). (3) Coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis); viridans streptococci are the other frequent cause when the aneurysm is embolic from endocarditis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mycotic aneurysm microbiology does not appear in the supplied pages; answer is from standard sources.

cohort_answer.text: Staph aureus; Salmonella sp; Staph epi.

questions.question: A bench isolate is a gram-negative bacillus: indole negative, citrate negative, motile; KIA shows a small amount of H2S; lysine decarboxylase positive, ornithine decarboxylase negative, arginine dihydrolase negative.
questions.question_raw: Practical station: BacT (Powerpoint) isolate - GNB, indole negative, citrate negative, motile. KIA shows small amounts of H2S, lysine positive, ornithine negative, arginine negative.

parts.text: Expected result if phenylalanine deaminase were tested?

parts_raw.text: Expected result if phenylalanine deaminase tested?

questions.model_answer: a) Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Salmonella is motile, indole/citrate variable with H2S production and lysine positive; the combination of only a small amount of H2S with ornithine-negative reaction is characteristic of S. Typhi (unlike most nontyphoidal serovars, which are ornithine positive and produce abundant H2S). b) Negative. Salmonella is phenylalanine deaminase negative; a positive PDA points instead to Proteus, Providencia, or Morganella.
questions.beyond_mandell: Biochemical identification details are not in this chapter; based on standard clinical microbiology reference (e.g., Mandell microbiology/Murray).

questions.question: A patient with Salmonella enteritis has an isolate that is susceptible to ciprofloxacin and to ceftriaxone.
questions.question_raw:
Q45 (2008, 2011 PM)
Salmonella in a person with enteritis. Cipro (S), CTX (S)

parts.text: Is ciprofloxacin a good treatment choice in this patient?

parts_raw.text: A) Is Cipro a good Tx choice in this patient?

questions.model_answer: a) For uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis in an otherwise healthy host, no antimicrobial (including ciprofloxacin) is indicated: therapy does not shorten illness or fever and increases the risk of prolonged stool carriage, adverse effects, and resistance; management is rehydration. Antimicrobials should be reserved for high-risk patients (neonates, age >50 with atherosclerosis, immunosuppression, valvular/endovascular or significant joint disease, or invasive infection). If treatment is warranted, then yes, ciprofloxacin is an appropriate and generally preferred oral agent for a susceptible strain.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answered simply "yes," but the chapter stresses that antimicrobials are not indicated for uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis; ciprofloxacin is a good choice only if the patient meets criteria for treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Yes. Higher rates and longer time to defervescence seen with CTX compared with Cipro for fully susceptible strains (better at eradicating biliary carriage with Cipro)

questions.question: Match each microbiological description to the correct stool pathogen. Pathogen options: Vibrio cholerae, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas.
questions.question_raw: Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro descriptions (4) and pathogens (5 – Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas)

parts.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal-based selective media.
Micro 3 - non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative, curved gram-negative bacillus.
Micro 4 - non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative, biochemically inert.

parts_raw.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal something something
Micro 3 - NLF, catalase negative curved GNB

questions.model_answer: a) Campylobacter (e.g. C. jejuni) - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal- or blood-based selective media (Skirrow/CCDA) at 42 degrees C. b) Salmonella typhimurium - H2S producing (black colonies on XLD/Hektoen/SS agar), non-lactose fermenter. c) Vibrio cholerae - non-lactose fermenter, comma/curved gram-negative rod, oxidase-positive facultative anaerobe growing on TCBS/alkaline peptone water. d) Shigella sonnei - non-lactose (or late-lactose) fermenting, non-motile, biochemically inert enteric. Aeromonas is the unused distractor.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Vibrio descriptors (curved GNR, oxidase-positive, selective media) are in this chapter; the Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella identifications rest on standard clinical microbiology (Mandell species chapters / Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

cohort_answer.text:
Campylobacter
Salmonella typhimurium
Vibrio
Shigella sonnei

questions.question: A patient from the Caribbean presents with repeated gram-negative bacillary bacteremia.
questions.question_raw: Q26 (2013 PM). From Caribbean, repeat GNB bacteremia.

parts.text: Three steps in the pathogenesis of the causative organism?
What testing will confirm your diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: B) 3 steps in the pathogenesis of the causative organism?
C) What testing will confirm your diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: a) Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis. In a patient from a Strongyloides-endemic region (Caribbean), recurrent enteric gram-negative bacteremia is the classic clue: migrating filariform larvae carry gut flora into the bloodstream. b) (1) Filariform larvae penetrate skin (or perianal skin in autoinfection) and migrate via blood/lymphatics to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed. (2) In the small intestine they mature to adult females that produce eggs hatching into rhabditiform larvae. (3) Rhabditiform larvae transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut and reinvade the intestinal mucosa/perianal skin (autoinfection); under immunosuppression this cycle amplifies massively, disseminating larvae and translocating enteric GNB into the blood. c) Serial concentrated stool examination for larvae (plus sputum/duodenal aspirate in hyperinfection), and Strongyloides serology. d) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg daily; extend until stool and sputum are negative for ~2 weeks in hyperinfection/dissemination (add albendazole in disseminated disease), and reduce or reverse immunosuppression.
questions.beyond_mandell: Not covered in the Salmonella chapter; answer rests on standard ID knowledge and the Mandell Strongyloides chapter/IDSA guidance.

cohort_answer.text:
Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome
Filariform larvae in soil penetrate human skin and migrate to small intestine; Larvae migrate via bloodstream and lymphatics to lungs where they are eventually coughed and swallowed; In the small intestine, they become female adult worms that produce eggs in the intestinal mucosa that become rhabditiform larvae; Rhabditiform larvae in the gut become infective filariform larvae that can penetrate either the intestinal mucosa or the skin of the perianal area, resulting in autoinfection.
Concentrated stool examination for microscopy (larvae/eggs)
Hyperinfection: ivermectin x 7 days; Disseminated: Ivermectin + albendazole daily until stool/ sputum is neg x 2 weeks; Reduce immunosuppression

questions.question: According to CLSI 2016, which three antibiotics should be routinely tested and reported for Salmonella and Shigella isolated from stool (report for fecal typhoidal Salmonella [Typhi and Paratyphi] and Shigella)?
questions.question_raw: According to CLSI 2016, which 3 antibiotics should be tested and reported for Salmonella and Shigella isolated from stool? Report only for fecal typhoidal salmonella (typhi and paratyphi), and shigella.
questions.model_answer: (1) Ampicillin. (2) A fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin). (3) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. For extraintestinal Salmonella isolates, a third-generation cephalosporin (and chloramphenicol) should additionally be reported.
questions.beyond_mandell: Based on CLSI M100 (2016) reporting guidance, not the chapter text.

cohort_answer.text: Ampicillin, Fluoroquinolones, Septra (if extraintestinal, also report 3rd gen cephalosporins; azithro has breakpoints now but not reported)

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. (A) Enterococcus faecium with MIC >256 for both teicoplanin and vancomycin. (B) Salmonella enteritidis with a resistance phenotype. (C) Enterobacter cloacae resistant to cephalosporins.
questions.question_raw: Q54 (2006 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. A) E. faecium with MIC >256 for both teicoplanin and vancomycin. B) Salmonella enteritidis (resistance stem unclear). C) Enterobacter cloacae resistant to cephalosporins

parts.text: Mechanism for Enterococcus faecium high-level vancomycin/teicoplanin resistance.

parts_raw.text: A) Mechanism for E. faecium high-level vanco/teicoplanin resistance
C) E. cloacae cephalosporin resistance mechanism

questions.model_answer: a) VanA-type resistance: acquisition of the vanA gene cluster reprograms peptidoglycan precursor synthesis so terminal D-Ala-D-Ala is replaced by D-Ala-D-Lac, drastically lowering glycopeptide binding; this confers high-level vancomycin resistance with cross-resistance to teicoplanin. b) Not covered in this chapter - typically plasmid-mediated multidrug resistance (e.g., an IncH1 plasmid carrying ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance). c) Not covered in this chapter - chromosomal (often derepressed) AmpC beta-lactamase, an Ambler class C cephalosporinase.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b (Salmonella plasmid-mediated resistance) and c (Enterobacter AmpC class C cephalosporinase) are general microbiology, not in this Enterococcus chapter.

cohort_answer.text: A) VanA gene acquisition - mediates high level vanco resistance by target modification to D-ala-D-lac; most common type, usually higher level resistance, cross-resistance to teicoplanin. B) Incompatible (Inc) plasmids - IncH1 plasmid acquisition leads to concurrent resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, TMP/SMX. C) Class C - AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal).

questions.question: Match each stool pathogen to its microbiological features. Features: (i) microaerophilic, grows on charcoal; (ii) H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative (possibly oxidase-negative) curved gram-negative bacillus; (iii) non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative (possibly oxidase-negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas.
questions.question_raw:
Q41 (2013 AM)
Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro features given: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal; H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB; NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas

parts.text: Match each pathogen to its microbiological features.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Microaerophilic, grows on charcoal = Campylobacter (spiral/vibrioid gram-negative rod, thermophilic 42 C, oxidase and catalase positive, requires microaerobic incubation and selective/charcoal media). (2) H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter = Salmonella typhimurium (facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, oxidase-negative, produces H2S). (3) Non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative/oxidase-negative = Shigella sonnei (nonmotile, no H2S). Vibrio and Aeromonas are oxidase-positive non-lactose fermenters and do not fit these three cues.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Campylobacter microbiology (microaerophilic, charcoal/selective media, oxidase/catalase-positive vibrioid morphology) is from this chapter; the Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio and Aeromonas features rest on standard clinical microbiology (Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

cohort_answer.text: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal - Campylobacter. H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB - Salmonella. NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative) - Shigella. Additional detail: Vibrio - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, curved-rod (comma) shape, facultative anaerobe, oxidase positive, motile with polar flagella. Shigella sonnei - nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic GNR, non-lactose fermenter, no H2S, indole positive, ferments glucose/urea, oxidase negative, differentiated by ornithine decarboxylase expression. Salmonella typhimurium - gram negative facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase negative, produces H2S. Campylobacter - spiral shape, long flagella, mostly microaerophilic, thermophilic, nonfermentative, oxidase and catalase positive, urease negative (vs Helicobacter urease positive). Aeromonas - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, ferments glucose
